source.title: Tropical Cyclone Attributes in Sparse Autoencoder Features of an AI Weather Model
source.authors: Jia-Pei Liu; Rui-Dong Li; Ting Sun; Guang-Heng Ni

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses feature splitting and non-uniqueness as possible influences, but does not test whether increasing dictionary size splits features or whether child features partition a parent's inputs.
record.gate_note: No dictionary-size sweep, parent–child feature matching, directional similarity test, or test of whether child features cover a coarse feature's inputs is reported. The paper does measure how cyclone-attribute relations are distributed over SAE features and how that organization recurs across fits and layers; these results are recorded as findings that fit none of the listed versions. Discussion that dictionary size and sparsity may affect splitting is not a tested result.
record.test_reason: The study uses fixed-size (4,096-feature, K=32) TopK SAEs on GraphCast to measure how cyclone-attribute relations distribute across features, fits and layers. It never varies dictionary size, matches parent and child features, tests absorption, or compares objectives. It mentions feature splitting only as a possible influence: dictionary size and sparsity "may affect feature splitting and aggregation", which the authors say they did not test. It therefore does not test any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors find a distributed but partially bundled organization of cyclone-attribute relations that recurs across seeds and layers. Deeper-layer F1 leaders align better with the t+6 h state. They attribute seed differences possibly to splitting or merging but did not test sensitivity to size or sparsity.
record.recipe_differences: Uses TopK SAEs to measure cyclone-attribute correspondence and organization across features, fits, and layers; it does not perform a dictionary-size splitting comparison or the parent–child tests specified in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported organization varies in feature identity, ranking, and concentration across independent fits and processor layers. The authors state they did not test sensitivity to dictionary size, sparsity, or the F1-selected subset size.

fits_no_version.finding: At a fixed SAE size, cyclone position, intensity and pressure-structure relations are spread over multiple features (dictionary-wide N_eff 18.5, 703.1, 59.5). Position and pressure-structure overlap in a more concentrated set (N_shared 4.38). This organization recurs across five seeds and all 16 layers despite changing feature identity.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In GraphCast, cyclone physical-attribute relations are distributed but partly bundled across SAE features, and this organization recurs across independent SAE fits and processor layers without feature alignment.

record.problems: The evidence is confined to GraphCast and 2018–2019 cyclone states. The analysis uses predefined physical attributes and does not establish whether GraphCast relies on the readouts. The authors did not test sensitivity to dictionary size, sparsity, or selected-subset size, and did not align individual features across fits or layers.
record.rows_left_out: No other reported results were retained: lifecycle-specific values for feature f613 and the forecast-time alignment results concern cyclone readout correspondence, not dictionary-size splitting, feature geometry, or parent–child input partitioning.

untested.parts: No dictionary-size sweep, no coarse-to-fine feature replacement, no input-coverage or direction comparison.
No size-dependent splitting in large models or open SAE releases; GraphCast SAEs are one fixed size.
No nested families, parent-child geometry or concept hierarchy tested.
No parent/child firing or absorption test; no variation of size or sparsity.
No decomposition of larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents; no novel-latent count across sizes. Seed variation in feature identity is shown but is not dictionary-size variation.
No test of the sparsity objective as the source of splitting; no Matryoshka or other objective comparison.

record.verdict_notes: Feature splitting appears only in the Discussion, as a speculative explanation of seed-to-seed differences. Seed dependence of features relates to the literature cited there (Paulo & Belrose; Leask et al.), not to the size-based versions here. The rows are correctly unlinked.

versions.untested_parts: No increasing-dictionary-size comparison, feature replacement, input coverage/partition test, or direction comparison.
The paper examines GraphCast layers and independent SAE fits, but does not test size-related splitting in large models or open SAE releases.
No nested feature families, child–parent geometry, or concept hierarchy is tested.
No parent/child firing or absorption test, and no variation of SAE size or sparsity to assess absorption.
The paper does not decompose larger-SAE latents into smaller-SAE latents or measure novel latents across dictionary sizes.
The paper notes size and sparsity as possible influences but does not test the sparsity objective as the source of splitting or compare objectives such as Matryoshka SAEs.

rows.subject: GraphCast, five independent SAE fits at each processor layer
rows.operation_detail: Compared the distribution and overlap of cyclone-attribute relations across processor depth without aligning features.

conditions.value: five independent SAE fits per layer

rows.measure: Recurrence of distributed but partially bundled attribute organization across depth
rows.value: The paper reports that the organization remained detectable throughout processor depth; feature identity, ranking, and concentration varied.
rows.note: This is recurrence of attribute-relation organization, not a test of size-dependent feature splitting.
rows.check: Qualitative recurrence statement with no numeric value; it does not bear on splitting.
